rotational-kinetic-energy-s2.title: Energy stored in a flywheel
rotational-kinetic-energy-s2.text: An engineer measures the energy stored in a flywheel (from the work needed to spin it up from rest on a frictionless bearing) at four angular velocities.

items.q: What is the rotational inertia of the turntable and clay together about the axle?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the disk alone. Add the clay as a point object, mr².
Value: that uses MR² for the disk. A solid disk has I = ½MR² (given).

why.correct: I = ½MR² + mr² = ½(3.0 kg)(0.20 m)² + (0.10 kg)(0.15 m)² = 0.0600 + 0.00225 = 0.06225 kg·m², about 0.062 kg·m² (the data have two significant figures).

items.q: What is the rotational kinetic energy of the turntable and clay? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: ω was not squared. K = ½Iω².
Value: the ½ is missing. K = ½Iω².

why.correct: K = ½Iω² = ½(0.06225 kg·m²)(6.0 rad/s)² = 1.12 J, about 1.1 J.

items.q: The turntable’s center does not move. Which statement about its kinetic energy is correct?
options: It has kinetic energy, because every piece of it is moving
It has no kinetic energy, because its center of mass is at rest
It has no kinetic energy, because opposite sides cancel out
Its kinetic energy is at the rim, where the speed is largest

why.correct: Each piece of mass moves at v = rω and has ½mv². Kinetic energy is a scalar, so these add up (to ½Iω²) even though the velocities point in different directions and the center does not move.
options: Right: K = ½Iω² counts the motion of every piece around the axle.
A body can have rotational kinetic energy while its center of mass stays put.
Velocities cancel in the total momentum, but kinetic energy is a scalar; it never cancels.
Every piece moves (v = rω) and contributes ½mv²; the rim pieces just contribute most.

items.q: The turntable is sped up to 12 rad/s. Its rotational kinetic energy becomes
options: 4 times as large
2 times as large
the same
8 times as large

why.correct: K = ½Iω² with I fixed, so doubling ω multiplies K by 4 (to about 4.5 J).
options: Right: K ∝ ω², and (2)² = 4.
K depends on ω², not ω.
A faster spin has more kinetic energy.
There is no cube: K = ½Iω².

items.q: What share of the total rotational kinetic energy belongs to the clay?

why.correct: Every part shares ω, so each part’s share of ½Iω² is its share of I: 0.00225/0.06225 = 3.6%.
options: Right: the clay’s I is 0.00225 of 0.06225 kg·m², and they share ω.
That is the clay’s share of the total mass (0.10 of 3.1 kg); energy depends on I, not mass alone.
That compares the distances 0.15 m and 0.20 m; I also depends on mass.
The clay and the disk do not share the energy equally; they have different I.

items.q: Which graph of these data gives a straight line through the origin?
options: K against ω²
K against ω
K against 1/ω
√K against ω²

why.correct: K = ½Iω², so K against ω² is a straight line through the origin with slope ½I.
options: Right: K = (½I)ω² is proportional to ω².
K rises faster than ω; the points curve upward.
K increases with ω, so it falls along a curve against 1/ω.
√K is proportional to ω, not ω².

items.q: Use the data to find the flywheel’s rotational inertia.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the slope of K against ω², which is ½I. Double it.
Value: that divides by ω instead of ω². K = ½Iω², so I = 2K/ω².

why.correct: From any row, I = 2K/ω²: for example 2(640 J)/(40 rad/s)² = 0.80 kg·m². The slope of K against ω² is ½I = 0.40 kg·m².

items.q: Predict the flywheel’s kinetic energy at 50 rad/s.

why.correct: K = ½Iω² = ½(0.80 kg·m²)(50 rad/s)² = 1000 J. The steps between rows grow (120, 200, 280 J), as a square law predicts.
options: Right: K = ½(0.80 kg·m²)(50 rad/s)² = 1000 J.
This scales 640 J by 50/40, as if K were proportional to ω.
This adds the last step (280 J) again, but each step is larger than the one before.
This forgets the ½I and uses ω² alone.

items.q: An engineer wants a flywheel of the same mass and radius to store more energy at the same ω. She should
options: move more of its mass to the rim
move more of its mass toward the axle
make it a solid disk instead of a ring
leave the shape, since K depends on mass

why.correct: At a fixed ω, K = ½Iω² is proportional to I. Putting the same mass farther from the axle raises I, so a rim-heavy flywheel stores more energy.
options: Right: that raises I, and K = ½Iω² rises with it.
That lowers I and so lowers the stored energy.
A solid disk has less of its mass at the rim than a ring of the same mass and radius.
K depends on I, which depends on where the mass is, not mass alone.
a scalar, measured in joules
a vector along the axis, in joules
a scalar, measured in N·m/s
a vector, measured in kg·m²/s

why.correct: K = ½Iω² is energy: a scalar, in joules (kg·m²/s² = J). A wheel turning clockwise or counterclockwise at the same rate has the same K.
options: Right: ½Iω² has no direction.
Energy has no direction; only the sign of ω does.
N·m/s is a watt, a unit of power.
kg·m²/s is the unit of a different rotational quantity.

items.q: A small flywheel with rotational inertia 0.050 kg·m² spins at 300 rad/s. How much kinetic energy does it store?

mistakes.why: Value: ω was not squared. K = ½Iω².

why.correct: K = ½Iω² = ½(0.050 kg·m²)(300 rad/s)² = 2250 J, about 2.3 kJ.

items.q: A wheel with rotational inertia 0.40 kg·m² has 25 J of rotational kinetic energy. How fast is it turning?

mistakes.why: Value: that is ω². Take the square root.
Value: the ½ was dropped. ω = √(2K/I).

items.q: A solid disk and a hoop of the same mass and radius spin at the same angular velocity about their centers (disk I = ½MR², hoop I = MR², given). Compared with the disk, the hoop has
options: twice the rotational kinetic energy
the same rotational kinetic energy
half the rotational kinetic energy
four times the rotational kinetic energy

why.correct: K = ½Iω². At the same ω the ratio of energies is the ratio of inertias: MR² ÷ ½MR² = 2.
options: Right: same ω, twice the I.
Same mass and ω, but the hoop’s mass is all at the rim, so its I is larger.
The hoop has the larger I, not the smaller.
K is proportional to I at fixed ω, and I doubles.

items.q: A figure skater spins on frictionless ice. Ignoring her arms, she is modeled as a cylinder. Predict how each quantity changes if, at the same angular velocity, she were twice as wide (same mass, cylinder radius doubled).

variables.name: Her rotational inertia
variables.why: I = ½MR² for a cylinder; doubling R at the same mass gives 4 times the I.

variables.name: Her rotational kinetic energy
variables.why: K = ½Iω²; with ω the same and I four times as large, K is four times as large.

variables.name: The angular velocity she would need to keep her original rotational kinetic energy
variables.why: K = ½Iω²; with I four times as large, the same K needs ω² one quarter as large, so half the angular velocity.

why.correct: Spreading the same mass farther from the axis raises I (as R²). At the same ω, K = ½Iω² rises in proportion to I; to keep the old K she would need half the angular velocity.

items.q: A solid cylinder of mass 0.60 kg and radius 0.15 m (I = ½MR², given) spins at 20 rad/s about its central axis. What is its rotational kinetic energy?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses MR². A solid cylinder has I = ½MR².
Value: R was not squared in I = ½MR².

items.q: Why does a spinning wheel’s rotational kinetic energy not depend on whether it turns clockwise or counterclockwise?
options: ω is squared, so its sign drops out
Kinetic energy depends on the mass and not the motion
The two directions have different rotational inertias
Clockwise turning has negative kinetic energy

why.correct: K = ½Iω², and squaring removes the sign of ω. Kinetic energy is a scalar and never negative.
options: Right: (−ω)² = ω².
It depends on I and ω, but not on the sign of ω.
I depends on the mass and axis, not the direction of turning.
Kinetic energy is never negative.
